before:
An HTTP handler receives an http.ResponseWriter and *http.Request. Set headers before WriteHeader or the first body write; the first body write would otherwise imply status 200. Once headers are committed, later header edits generally cannot change the response already sent.

w.Header() takes no arguments and returns the mutable header map associated with this pending response. Set updates that map; do so before committing status or body, not after the response has begun.

httptest.NewRequest constructs an in-memory incoming request, and NewRecorder records handler output. Calling handler directly performs no HTTP network request. This example accepts GET and returns a 405 rejection with an Allow: GET header for other methods; fmt.Fprint’s write error is checked, although the in-memory recorder does not simulate a broken network connection.

Expected output or behavior: 200
ready. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Add a supported method deliberately and explain when the status becomes committed. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: HTTP is a set of rules for requests and replies. A handler reads a request and writes a response. Headers describe the reply; the status code gives its outcome; the body holds its content. Set headers before writing the status or body. A first body write would otherwise imply status 200.

httptest makes a request and records the handler's reply in memory. GET is allowed here. Other methods receive status 405 and an Allow header naming GET. The handler checks its body-write error, though this recorder does not test a broken network connection.
The screen shows `200`, then `ready`. The GET request takes the success path.
For an unsupported method, the handler sets Allow, writes the 405 error response, and returns. It never reaches the success body.
